doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Organ work, singers and Russia tour
title: Joe Williams and finding an Eubie Blake song
summary: Hyman calls Joe Williams the greatest jazz singer; while musical director for an Eubie Blake tribute he found a song Joe loved.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Do you have any stories that you could tell us about perhaps some gigs you’ve done with Joe Williams?

Well, Joe, first of all I think that Joe is the greatest jazz singer there ever was. And I think his sense of time is just about as good as any great drummer in the business. And the funny thing was that one of the things that I did with Joe I didn’t play on at all, but we were doing a show in tribute to Eubie Blake called “Eubie’s Hundred Years” or something like that. It was on the occasion of his hundredth birthday. It was a show on public television out of Washington. Joe was one of the guests and part of the job, of my job as musical director, was locating music, old Eubie Blake music obviously. And in Eubie’s files in his old brownstone house in Brooklyn, among a lot of other music, we found something called “I’d Give a Dollar for a Dime” with lyrics by Andy Razaf. It turned out to be a very nice, even plaintive song and very period in a tender sense because it’s been a long time since anybody needed a dime for a jukebox. And Joe loved the song. But as I say, I didn’t accompany him on it on the show, Frank Owens did. I was busy doing other things. It was one of the nicest moments on the show. Since then I have played that song with Joe on one or another occasion. He’s just a very nice man in addition to his great talent. A nice gentleman.
